findings.issue_text: [BUG] The script uses BSD/macOS-only sed in-place syntax `sed -i '' -E "s|...|...|"` which breaks on Linux (GNU sed treats the separate '' argument inconsistently and this form fails or corrupts the -E flag handling), so the declared cross-platform dev workflow only works on macOS. Any developer running this script on Linux gets a sed error or wrong substitution, leaving GOOGLE_WEBHOOK_URL stale so Google webhooks point at an old tunnel URL and never reach the local dev server.

[ADVISORY] The script invokes `tmole` with no dependency added anywhere in the diff (no package.json entry, no bootstrap/README change), assuming the tunnelmole binary is already installed globally on PATH. A developer running `scripts/test-gcal-webhooks.sh` on a fresh checkout gets 'command not found'; the script silently exits via cleanup with no actionable message pointing at installing tunnelmole.

[ADVISORY] ENV_FILE is hardcoded to the relative path `../.env`, which is only correct when the script is invoked with the scripts/ directory as the working directory; running it from the repo root writes/edits a non-existent or wrong .env file. A developer who runs `./scripts/test-gcal-webhooks.sh` from the repo root gets the '⚠️ ../.env not found. Creating new file' path and the generated GOOGLE_WEBHOOK_URL lands in a stray .env at the repo root, never read by the app, so webhook testing fails with no obvious cause.

[ADVISORY] The dev:cron script replaces the local dependency ts-node with `npx tsx`, but `tsx` is not declared as a dependency of apps/web in this diff, so npx performs a runtime network fetch of an unpinned version from the npm registry. Running dev:cron offline or in a sandboxed CI environment fails with a registry error, and the tsx version used drifts over time since no version is pinned in package.json.

[BUG] updateManyByCredentialId is called with empty data ({}) from CalendarService.ts:1022-1023 for ALL SelectedCalendars under the credential, bumping updatedAt even for calendars whose availability was never refreshed in that run, so the 'Last updated: {{timestamp}}' shown in CredentialActionsDropdown reflects watch-renewal time, not actual cache freshness. Users see a cache-status timestamp that claims data is fresh when the underlying CalendarCache entries were never rewritten (e.g. the per-calendar refresh loop was skipped or partially executed), defeating the stated purpose of the feature.

[BUG] deleteCacheMutation.onSuccess only shows a toast and calls onSuccess but never invalidates utils.viewer.calendars.connectedCalendars (unlike disconnectMutation which does on line 58-59), so after deleting the cache the dropdown continues rendering the pre-delete cacheUpdatedAt until an unrelated refetch happens. User deletes cached data, sees 'Cache deleted successfully', but the UI still shows the old 'Last updated' timestamp, making the delete appear to have failed.

[BUG] The not-found path throws a bare Error('Credential not found or access denied'), which tRPC surfaces as an HTTP 500 INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR instead of a 404/403, and the client's onError handler shows the generic 'error_deleting_cache' string regardless. A user passing another user's credentialId (or a stale id) triggers a 500, polluting error monitoring and giving the client no actionable code to distinguish denial from server failure.

[ADVISORY] The handler unconditionally instantiates the concrete CalendarCacheRepository and issues a groupBy query on every connectedCalendars fetch, ignoring the repository mock/disabled path that the calendar-cache feature provides (calendar-cache.repository.mock.ts exists precisely for the disabled case but this handler bypasses it). Every connectedCalendars read (including onboarding and settings pages) pays an extra DB groupBy even when the calendar-cache feature flag is off, and the disabled-flag behavior divergence is invisible until someone wires the mock in.

[ADVISORY] No test in this diff covers deleteCache.handler, getCacheStatusByCredentialIds, the updatedAt bump in CalendarService, or CredentialActionsDropdown — the diff adds a new mutation route, a new repository method, and a new component with zero spec/test files. A regression in ownership scoping on deleteCache (e.g. dropping the userId filter) would ship silently; the mock repository (calendar-cache.repository.mock.ts) returns [] untested, masking contract drift with the interface.

[ADVISORY] The cache-status timestamp is formatted with a hardcoded 'en-US' Intl.DateTimeFormat, ignoring the user's locale that useLocale already provides. Non-English users see dates formatted in US style (MM/DD/YY) everywhere else in the app localizes, an inconsistent rendering on the touched rendering path.

[ADVISORY] Both the delete-cache item and the remove-app item use StartIcon='trash' with color='destructive' and near-identical presentation, relying on text alone to distinguish an irreversible data deletion from an account disconnect. Users confirming the danger dialog can't visually distinguish which destructive action they initiated if the dropdown was closed before the dialog appears, increasing mis-delete risk on two destructive paths sharing one visual language.

[ADVISORY] hasCache is gated solely on integrationType === GOOGLE_CALENDAR_TYPE, hard-coding the gcal assumption into a generic-sounding component while the cache repository method it depends on is credential-agnostic. When a second calendar provider gains cache status (the repository and tRPC endpoint already support any credentialId), this component silently hides the status for those credentials; the next change must touch this hardcoded comparison, a parallel-enumeration smell.

[ADVISORY] A brand-new 79-line Tunnelmole tunneling dev script for GCal webhooks is included in a PR whose stated intent is 'add calendar cache status and actions'. Reviewers and release owners must vet unrelated tooling (writes to ../.env via sed, spawns background processes) as part of a feature change; it is not traceable to any requirement in the PR title and bloats the change surface that must be regression-checked.

[ADVISORY] The dev:cron script change from ts-node to npx tsx is unrelated work smuggled into the cache-status PR. Not traceable to the stated intent; if tsx behavior differs (config resolution, ESM handling) the cron-tester workflow changes with no requirement justifying the risk, and it silently alters every developer's cron-testing path.

[BUG] fetchAvailabilityAndCache silently mutates SelectedCalendar.updatedAt for ALL calendars under the credential on every availability fetch, work not traceable to the cache-status UI requirement and a hidden write amplification on the availability hot path. Every free-busy fetch (a hot, per-booking path) now issues an unconditional DB updateMany across every SelectedCalendar row for the credential, adding write load and contention; the UI 'Last updated' timestamp shown to users becomes the time of the last availability fetch by ANY user triggering this credential, not a meaningful per-calendar signal. The empty data object {} relies on Prisma's @updatedAt side effect, an undocumented coupling that breaks silently if the field annotation changes.

[ADVISORY] findMany is refactored to drop the satisfies-checked args object, an untraceable drive-by refactor inside a feature PR. The `satisfies Prisma.SelectedCalendarFindManyArgs` compile-time guard that previously caught shape drift between {where, select, orderBy} callers and the Prisma API is removed for no feature reason; the next caller passing a mistyped arg loses that static check.

[ADVISORY] updatedAt and googleChannelId are added to the UserWithCalendars SelectedCalendar picks (and to the UserRepository select in packages/lib/server/repository/user.ts:899-901), but no code in this diff reads googleChannelId or consumes these SelectedCalendar-level fields — the UI uses credential-level CalendarCache.updatedAt instead. Two new fields are fetched for every selected calendar row on every connected-calendars query with zero consumers in this diff — dead payload weight on a frequently-called query, and a misleading type contract suggesting SelectedCalendar.updatedAt drives the cache display when it is actually CalendarCache.updatedAt; the next developer touching this code must reverse-engineer which timestamp is real.

[ADVISORY] deleteCacheHandler bypasses the calendar-cache repository abstraction and hand-rolls prisma.calendarCache.deleteMany, even though ICalendarCacheRepository already exposes deleteManyByCredential (see calendar-cache.repository.interface.ts and the mock that implements it). Two parallel deletion paths now exist: the feature-scoped repository (with its cache-disabled mock semantics used by platform atoms) and a raw Prisma call in the tRPC handler; when cache deletion semantics change (e.g. soft-delete, event propagation, or the disabled-cache guard), the tRPC path silently diverges from the mocked/platform path, and the mock-based tests no longer represent handler behavior.

[BUG] A non-owned or missing credentialId throws a generic Error, surfacing as an untyped 500 instead of a NOT_FOUND/FORBIDDEN tRPC error. When a user submits a stale or foreign credentialId (e.g. after the credential was deleted in another tab), the client's onError shows 'Error deleting cache' with no distinguishable status, and the error lands in 5xx monitoring as a server fault for what is a 4xx-class client condition.

[ADVISORY] Every connectedCalendars fetch now unconditionally constructs a CalendarCacheRepository and runs a groupBy query, even when the calendar-cache feature is disabled (the state the CalendarCacheRepositoryMock exists to represent). The cache-status read is not gated behind the same enablement flag the rest of the calendar-cache feature uses, so deployments with calendar-cache disabled pay a DB query per settings-page load and get an empty map (dropdown hides cache items) — the feature gate and the UI affordance can disagree about whether caching is active.

[BUG] deleteCacheHandler throws a plain Error('Credential not found or access denied') instead of a TRPCError, so a bad or foreign credentialId surfaces as a tRPC INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR (500) instead of a 4xx the contract implies. Any client calling deleteCache with a credentialId the user doesn't own (or a stale one after disconnect) gets a 500 error logged as a server fault, polluting error monitoring with expected user-input failures instead of a clean NOT_FOUND response.

[BUG] The cache-status refresh mechanism is a no-op: SelectedCalendarRepository.updateManyByCredentialId(this.credential.id, {}) is called with empty data, so no field (including updatedAt) is ever written. The comment claims it 'updates SelectedCalendar.updatedAt', but an updateMany with an empty data object performs no write (or throws validation), so SelectedCalendar.updatedAt never reflects a cache refresh and any UI or logic relying on it to show cache freshness is permanently stale — the whole refresh-timestamp feature this call exists for does not work.

[ADVISORY] deleteCacheHandler deletes via prisma.calendarCache.deleteMany directly, bypassing CalendarCacheRepository.deleteManyByCredential which exists as the abstraction (with a feature-disabled mock path) for exactly this operation. Two parallel service paths now write to the calendar cache: the repository (feature-flag-aware, mockable) and this raw prisma call. When the calendar-cache feature is disabled in a deployment, the mock suppresses deletes but this handler still hard-deletes rows, and any future change to cache storage (e.g. keying, soft-delete) must be updated in two places or they drift.

[ADVISORY] deleteCacheMutation's onSuccess shows a toast and calls onSuccess but never invalidates the connectedCalendars query, unlike disconnectMutation which invalidates in onSettled. After a user deletes cached data, the dropdown continues to display 'Last updated: <old timestamp>' from the stale tRPC cache until an unrelated refetch happens, making the delete appear to have done nothing to the very status indicator this feature adds.

[ADVISORY] The migration backfills every legacy CalendarCache row with updatedAt = NOW() (the migration run time), which is a fabricated timestamp bearing no relation to when the cache entry was actually written. After deploy, every user with an existing cache sees 'Last updated: <deploy time>' — a misleading cache-status display that can hide genuinely stale caches, since nothing distinguishes a fresh entry from a legacy backfilled one.

[ADVISORY] connectedCalendarsHandler always instantiates and calls CalendarCacheRepository.getCacheStatusByCredentialIds unconditionally, even in deployments where the calendar-cache feature is disabled (the repository mock exists solely for that case). Every connectedCalendars fetch on every settings/onboarding page load pays an extra groupBy query and enriches every calendar with a cacheUpdatedAt that the disabled feature never maintains, exposing a meaningless 'Last updated' timestamp to users of disabled-cache deployments.

[ADVISORY] cacheUpdatedAt crosses the tRPC boundary where Dates are JSON-serialized to strings, but the prop is typed as Date | null and 'new Date(cacheUpdatedAt)' re-wraps it; the compile-time type asserts a type the wire format does not deliver. The prop's Date type is a lie on the client side; any future code treating it as a real Date (e.g. calling toISOString or date math on it without re-wrapping) breaks at runtime, and the re-wrapping in the render is load-bearing in a non-obvious way.

[ADVISORY] findMany drops the `satisfies Prisma.SelectedCalendarFindManyArgs` type check, silently weakening the compile-time contract on the args passed through to prisma. The next caller passing a malformed where/select now gets no type error at this boundary (previously caught by the satisfies clause), so a query-shape mistake surfaces only as a runtime Prisma error or as silently returning more columns than intended.

[BUG] deleteCacheHandler throws a plain Error('Credential not found or access denied') for a valid-but-unowned credentialId, which tRPC maps to a 500 INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR instead of a 4xx the client contract expects. A user probing another user's credentialId (or a stale UI after the credential was deleted) gets a generic 500 logged as a server error; the client's onError shows 'Error deleting cache' with no distinguishable cause, and error trackers fill with false-positive 500s from an expected authorization rejection.

[ADVISORY] deleteCacheMutation.onSuccess shows a toast and calls onSuccess but never invalidates utils.viewer.calendars.connectedCalendars, unlike the sibling disconnectMutation which invalidates it in onSettled. After deleting cache, the ConnectedCalendars query still holds the old cacheUpdatedAt, so the 'Last updated' row keeps displaying the pre-delete timestamp until some other action refetches — the success toast contradicts the visible state.

[ADVISORY] connectedCalendarsHandler hard-instantiates `new CalendarCacheRepository()`, bypassing the repository-interface/mock abstraction the same PR extends (calendar-cache.repository.mock.ts returns [] precisely for the cache-disabled case). Every connectedCalendars fetch now runs an unconditional calendarCache.groupBy DB query even where the calendar-cache feature is disabled or mocked out; the DI seam the codebase maintains for this feature (interface + mock added in this diff) is silently skipped, so tests against the mock no longer reflect the real handler path and disabled-cache deployments pay a dead query on a hot settings-page path.

[ADVISORY] The new code updates SelectedCalendar.updatedAt for all calendars under the credential, but the cache-status UI introduced in this same PR reads CalendarCache.updatedAt (via getCacheStatusByCredentialIds), so the two halves of the feature target different tables. The updateManyByCredentialId write in fetchAvailabilityAndSetCache has no consumer in this diff's UI path — it mutates SelectedCalendar rows on every cron refresh, repurposing SelectedCalendar.updatedAt's meaning (selection-change timestamp) for cache bookkeeping nobody displays, while whoever later wires SelectedCalendar.updatedAt into the status card will double-count refreshes since CalendarCache.updatedAt is already maintained by @updatedAt on every setAvailabilityInCache upsert.

[ADVISORY] The timestamp is formatted with a hardcoded 'en-US' Intl.DateTimeFormat locale instead of the user's active locale from useLocale(). Non-English users see the only user-visible dynamic string in the dropdown rendered in US date/time format, contradicting the PR's own i18n setup (locale strings were added to common.json for every other label in this component).

[ADVISORY] cacheUpdatedAt is typed `Date | null` but arrives over the tRPC HTTP boundary as a serialized string, so `new Date(cacheUpdatedAt)` at line 106 relies on an untyped runtime value the declared type doesn't describe. Any consumer trusting the Date type (e.g. calling Date methods directly or passing the prop onward) hits runtime string behavior; the type lie propagates to every future caller of the component, and superjson-vs-JSON transport changes would silently alter what `new Date(cacheUpdatedAt)` receives.

[ADVISORY] The script uses `sed -i ''` (BSD/macOS-only syntax) and a CWD-relative ENV_FILE="../.env", so on Linux it rewrites the env file in-place incorrectly and from any directory other than scripts/ it edits the wrong .env. A developer running the script from the repo root on Linux gets a sed error or a corrupted .env line (sed treats '' as a filename), silently failing to point GOOGLE_WEBHOOK_URL at the tunnel and leaving gcal webhook testing broken with no visible error.

[ADVISORY] deleteCacheHandler throws a plain Error('Credential not found or access denied') instead of a TRPCError, so an invalid credentialId surfaces as a generic 500 rather than a 4xx and the raw message can leak in the error response Any authenticated caller probing credentialIds gets a 500-with-message path indistinguishable from server failure; the error string is emitted to client-facing error payloads in the tRPC default error formatter, and operators get noise instead of a typed NOT_FOUND

[ADVISORY] The deleteCache mutation accepts any credentialId owned by the user but does not verify the credential is a Google Calendar credential, and the handler deletes only calendarCache rows without clearing the in-memory/availability cache path that CalendarService reads A user deleting cache for a non-calendar credential gets success:true with no effect, and for a Google credential the next availability fetch may still be served by layers outside calendarCache that the handler does not purge, so the 'delete cached data' UI action is not a complete invalidation

[ADVISORY] The DEFAULT NOW() backfill stamps every legacy CalendarCache row with the migration-execution time, so pre-existing caches instantly appear 'fresh' as of deploy time. Users with stale cache entries see 'Last updated: <migration timestamp>' in the new cache-status UI and believe their availability data was just refreshed, defeating the purpose of the feature for all pre-existing rows; correct behavior would require seeding updatedAt from the cache creation signal (e.g. expiresAt minus TTL) rather than NOW(). No data is lost and the migration itself is reversible (DROP COLUMN), so this is not blocking.

[ADVISORY] updateManyByCredentialId is called with an empty data object ({}), relying entirely on Prisma's implicit @updatedAt behavior on SelectedCalendar to bump the timestamp — if SelectedCalendar.updatedAt lacks @updatedAt in the schema, the call is a silent no-op write. The CalendarService refresh hook (CalendarService.ts line ~1022) intends to mark all SelectedCalendars under the credential as refreshed; if the model's updatedAt is a plain DateTime without @updatedAt, Prisma rejects or ignores empty update data and SelectedCalendar.updatedAt never advances, so any future consumer reading SelectedCalendar.updatedAt (it is now surfaced in getConnectedDestinationCalendars and UserRepository select) sees stale timestamps. Verify @updatedAt is present on SelectedCalendar.updatedAt.

[BUG] deleteCacheHandler throws a plain Error('Credential not found or access denied') when the credential lookup misses, which tRPC surfaces as a 500 INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR instead of the 404/403 the situation calls for. A user (or a stale client holding a deleted credentialId) triggering 'Delete cached data' gets a generic server-error toast and a 5xx logged server-side for what is an expected not-found/forbidden case; error monitoring is polluted with non-exception failures.

[ADVISORY] deleteCacheMutation has no onSettled invalidation of viewer.calendars.connectedCalendars, so the displayed 'Last updated' timestamp stays stale unless the parent happens to pass an onSuccess prop that refetches. Any consumer of CredentialActionsDropdown that omits onSuccess (the prop is optional) shows the old cache timestamp after a successful delete until an unrelated refetch occurs, making the user believe the delete did nothing.

[ADVISORY] connectedCalendarsHandler directly instantiates CalendarCacheRepository instead of going through the calendar-cache feature factory, bypassing the CalendarCacheRepositoryMock used when the feature is disabled. When calendar-cache is disabled the handler still issues a groupBy query against calendarCache on every connectedCalendars fetch, and the disabled-mode contract ('skip and log') documented in calendar-cache.repository.mock.ts is silently not honored; deployments with the feature off pay a DB round-trip per settings/onboarding page load for data that is always empty.

[ADVISORY] Every getAvailability path now performs an unconditional updateMany write across all SelectedCalendar rows for the credential, even when availability was served from a still-valid cache and nothing was refreshed. Read-path availability checks turn into N-row writes on each call, adding DB write load and constantly churning SelectedCalendar.updatedAt for every calendar under the credential, degrading any other consumer that relies on updatedAt as a change signal.

This results in inaccurate cache status tracking, as the timestamp isn't updated when the cache is refreshed. To fix this, explicitly set the updatedAt field.
logic: macOS-specific sed syntax with empty string after -i flag will fail on Linux systems

Throwing a generic Error for authentication failures results in a 500 response in tRPC. Instead, it should return a structured TRPCError with an appropriate code, such as FORBIDDEN, to accurately reflect the error type.
Date is formatted with hardcoded 'en-US' locale instead of using the user's locale from useLocale, which can lead to incorrect date representation for users in different locales.

On a fresh checkout without `tmole` on PATH, the script’s core action cannot work and it will eventually hit the `Failed to extract Tunnelmole URL.` path without telling the user how to resolve the missing binary.

Because the script uses this path as-is (not relative to the script’s own location), the target file depends on the caller’s current working directory. Running `./scripts/test-gcal-webhooks.sh` from the repo root will make `../.env` point outside the repo, triggering the `"../.env not found. While the diff does not show whether `tsx` is already declared in `apps/web` dependencies, using `npx tsx` can fall back to downloading `tsx` at runtime if it isn’t installed locally, making the command less reproducible/offline-friendly. A reviewer could reasonably request ensuring `tsx` is pinned as a (dev)dependency and/or invoked via the local binary rather than relying on `npx` behavior.

It does not use `SelectedCalendar.updatedAt` at all. Therefore, even if `SelectedCalendarRepository.updateManyByCredentialId(this.credential.id, {})` were to bump `SelectedCalendar.updatedAt`, that would not affect the displayed “Last updated” cache status shown in the new dropdown.

adjudication.rationale: In `packages/trpc/server/routers/viewer/calendars/connectedCalendars.handler.ts`, the diff explicitly imports and unconditionally constructs `new CalendarCacheRepository()` and calls `getCacheStatusByCredentialIds(...)`, which performs a Prisma `groupBy` query. adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] No test in this diff covers deleteCache.handler, getCacheStatusByCredentialIds, the updatedAt bump in CalendarService, or CredentialActionsDropdown — the diff adds a new mutation route, a new repository method, and a new component with zero spec/test files. adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The cache-status timestamp is formatted with a hardcoded 'en-US' Intl.DateTimeFormat, ignoring the user's locale that useLocale already provides. [ADVISORY] Both the delete-cache item and the remove-app item use StartIcon='trash' with color='destructive' and near-identical presentation, relying on text alone to distinguish an irreversible data deletion from an account disconnect. Users confirming the danger dialog can't visually distinguish which destructive action they initiated if the dropdown was closed before the dialog appears, increasing mis-delete risk on two destructive paths sharing one visual language.

adjudication.rationale: In `packages/features/apps/components/CredentialActionsDropdown.tsx`, both destructive dropdown actions use the same visual treatment (`color="destructive"` and `StartIcon="trash"`) for two different operations: deleting cached data (opens `deleteModalOpen`) and removing the app/credential (opens `disconnectModalOpen`). While the dialogs do have different titles/text (`t("delete_cached_data")` vs `t("remove_app")`), the finding is a valid, diff-grounded UX-risk concern rather than a verifiable functional defect.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] hasCache is gated solely on integrationType === GOOGLE_CALENDAR_TYPE, hard-coding the gcal assumption into a generic-sounding component while the cache repository method it depends on is credential-agnostic. When a second calendar provider gains cache status (the repository and tRPC endpoint already support any credentialId), this component silently hides the status for those credentials; the next change must touch this hardcoded comparison, a parallel-enumeration smell.

adjudication.rationale: In `CredentialActionsDropdown`, `hasCache` is computed as `isGoogleCalendar && cacheUpdatedAt` (where `isGoogleCalendar` is `integrationType === GOOGLE_CALENDAR_TYPE`), so the cache status UI and the "Delete cached data" action are hidden for any non-Google integration even if `cacheUpdatedAt` is provided. This mismatch is a diff-grounded design/maintenance concern (future providers would require touching this hardcoded comparison), but it is not a verifiable current correctness defect given the diff does not show other providers actually using `CalendarCache`.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] A brand-new 79-line Tunnelmole tunneling dev script for GCal webhooks is included in a PR whose stated intent is 'add calendar cache status and actions'. This tooling is not directly related to the stated feature changes in the diff (calendar cache status/actions) and increases review/release surface area with side-effectful behavior, so reviewers should explicitly vet/justify its inclusion or split it out.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The dev:cron script change from ts-node to npx tsx is unrelated work smuggled into the cache-status PR. adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] fetchAvailabilityAndCache silently mutates SelectedCalendar.updatedAt for ALL calendars under the credential on every availability fetch, work not traceable to the cache-status UI requirement and a hidden write amplification on the availability hot path. Every free-busy fetch (a hot, per-booking path) now issues an unconditional DB updateMany across every SelectedCalendar row for the credential, adding write load and contention; the UI 'Last updated' timestamp shown to users becomes the time of the last availability fetch by ANY user triggering this credential, not a meaningful per-calendar signal. The empty data object {} relies on Prisma's @updatedAt side effect, an undocumented coupling that breaks silently if the field annotation changes.

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds an unconditional write on the availability hot path: in `GoogleCalendarService.fetchAvailabilityAndCache` it now calls `SelectedCalendarRepository.updateManyByCredentialId(this.credential.id, {})` for every fetch (comment says it’s to update `SelectedCalendar.updatedAt`). However, the finding’s claim about the cache-status UI timestamp being driven by this `SelectedCalendar.updatedAt` change is not supported by the diff (the UI uses `cacheUpdatedAt` derived from `CalendarCache.updatedAt`), so it’s not a clearly verifiable functional bug from what’s shown.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] findMany is refactored to drop the satisfies-checked args object, an untraceable drive-by refactor inside a feature PR. The `satisfies Prisma.SelectedCalendarFindManyArgs` compile-time guard that previously caught shape drift between {where, select, orderBy} callers and the Prisma API is removed for no feature reason; the next caller passing a mistyped arg loses that static check.

adjudication.rationale: In `packages/lib/server/repository/selectedCalendar.ts`, `SelectedCalendarRepository.findMany` was changed from building an `args` object with a `satisfies Prisma.SelectedCalendarFindManyArgs` compile-time check to directly calling `prisma.selectedCalendar.findMany({ where, select, orderBy })`. adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] updatedAt and googleChannelId are added to the UserWithCalendars SelectedCalendar picks (and to the UserRepository select in packages/lib/server/repository/user.ts:899-901), but no code in this diff reads googleChannelId or consumes these SelectedCalendar-level fields — the UI uses credential-level CalendarCache.updatedAt instead. adjudication.rationale: The diff does add `updatedAt` and `googleChannelId` to `UserWithCalendars`’s `SelectedCalendar` picks (packages/lib/getConnectedDestinationCalendars.ts) and selects those fields in `UserRepository` (packages/lib/server/repository/user.ts). No code in this diff reads `SelectedCalendar.updatedAt` or `googleChannelId`, so these added fields are currently unused payload/contract noise on a likely hot query and could mislead future readers about which timestamp drives the cache status.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] deleteCacheHandler bypasses the calendar-cache repository abstraction and hand-rolls prisma.calendarCache.deleteMany, even though ICalendarCacheRepository already exposes deleteManyByCredential (see calendar-cache.repository.interface.ts and the mock that implements it). Two parallel deletion paths now exist: the feature-scoped repository (with its cache-disabled mock semantics used by platform atoms) and a raw Prisma call in the tRPC handler; when cache deletion semantics change (e.g. soft-delete, event propagation, or the disabled-cache guard), the tRPC path silently diverges from the mocked/platform path, and the mock-based tests no longer represent handler behavior.

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds a new tRPC mutation `deleteCache` whose handler (`packages/trpc/server/routers/viewer/calendars/deleteCache.handler.ts`) directly calls `prisma.calendarCache.deleteMany({ where: { credentialId } })`. At the same time, the calendar-cache feature already defines an abstraction `ICalendarCacheRepository` with `deleteManyByCredential(...)` (and a mock implementation that no-ops when cache is disabled). adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] A non-owned or missing credentialId throws a generic Error, surfacing as an untyped 500 instead of a NOT_FOUND/FORBIDDEN tRPC error. When a user submits a stale or foreign credentialId (e.g. after the credential was deleted in another tab), the client's onError shows 'Error deleting cache' with no distinguishable status, and the error lands in 5xx monitoring as a server fault for what is a 4xx-class client condition.
matched_golden_ids: Throwing a generic Error for authentication failures results in a 500 response in tRPC. Instead, it should return a structured TRPCError with an appropriate code, such as FORBIDDEN, to accurately reflect the error type.
adjudication_records.primary_judge_reasoning: Both point out that throwing a generic Error causes tRPC to surface an untyped 500, and that the code should instead throw a structured TRPCError with an appropriate 4xx code (e.g., FORBIDDEN/NOT_FOUND) for unauthorized or missing resources.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] Every connectedCalendars fetch now unconditionally constructs a CalendarCacheRepository and runs a groupBy query, even when the calendar-cache feature is disabled (the state the CalendarCacheRepositoryMock exists to represent). The cache-status read is not gated behind the same enablement flag the rest of the calendar-cache feature uses, so deployments with calendar-cache disabled pay a DB query per settings-page load and get an empty map (dropdown hides cache items) — the feature gate and the UI affordance can disagree about whether caching is active.

adjudication.rationale: In `packages/trpc/server/routers/viewer/calendars/connectedCalendars.handler.ts`, the diff adds an unconditional `new CalendarCacheRepository()` and `getCacheStatusByCredentialIds(credentialIds)` call for every `connectedCalendars` request, and then always enriches results with `cacheUpdatedAt`. There is no feature-flag/enablement check shown here, and the mock repository (`CalendarCacheRepositoryMock`) is not used in this path, so the handler will always execute the Prisma `groupBy` query added in `calendar-cache.repository.ts`. This is a concrete perf/architecture concern (extra DB query + potential mismatch with whatever mechanism disables calendar-cache), but the diff alone doesn’t prove a functional correctness failure.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] deleteCacheHandler throws a plain Error('Credential not found or access denied') instead of a TRPCError, so a bad or foreign credentialId surfaces as a tRPC INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR (500) instead of a 4xx the contract implies. Any client calling deleteCache with a credentialId the user doesn't own (or a stale one after disconnect) gets a 500 error logged as a server fault, polluting error monitoring with expected user-input failures instead of a clean NOT_FOUND response.

adjudication.rationale: In `packages/trpc/server/routers/viewer/calendars/deleteCache.handler.ts`, when the credential lookup fails, the handler does `throw new Error("Credential not found or access denied")`. With the new `deleteCache` tRPC mutation (`_router.tsx`) there is no conversion to a `TRPCError`, so this will be treated as an unhandled/internal error by tRPC rather than a typed 4xx-style error (e.g., NOT_FOUND/FORBIDDEN). This matches the finding that expected user-input cases (stale/foreign `credentialId`) will surface as a server fault.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] The cache-status refresh mechanism is a no-op: SelectedCalendarRepository.updateManyByCredentialId(this.credential.id, {}) is called with empty data, so no field (including updatedAt) is ever written. The comment claims it 'updates SelectedCalendar.updatedAt', but an updateMany with an empty data object performs no write (or throws validation), so SelectedCalendar.updatedAt never reflects a cache refresh and any UI or logic relying on it to show cache freshness is permanently stale — the whole refresh-timestamp feature this call exists for does not work.
matched_golden_ids: The updateManyByCredentialId call uses an empty data object, which prevents Prisma's @updatedAt decorator from updating the updatedAt timestamp. This results in inaccurate cache status tracking, as the timestamp isn't updated when the cache is refreshed. To fix this, explicitly set the updatedAt field.
adjudication_records.primary_judge_reasoning: The candidate flags that updateManyByCredentialId is invoked with an empty data object, resulting in no write and therefore updatedAt not being updated, breaking cache freshness tracking. This is the same underlying issue described in the golden comment (and implies the same fix: explicitly set updatedAt).

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] deleteCacheHandler deletes via prisma.calendarCache.deleteMany directly, bypassing CalendarCacheRepository.deleteManyByCredential which exists as the abstraction (with a feature-disabled mock path) for exactly this operation. Two parallel service paths now write to the calendar cache: the repository (feature-flag-aware, mockable) and this raw prisma call. When the calendar-cache feature is disabled in a deployment, the mock suppresses deletes but this handler still hard-deletes rows, and any future change to cache storage (e.g. keying, soft-delete) must be updated in two places or they drift.

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds `deleteCacheHandler` which calls `prisma.calendarCache.deleteMany({ where: { credentialId } })` directly (new file `packages/trpc/server/routers/viewer/calendars/deleteCache.handler.ts`). In the same diff, an abstraction exists for cache operations (`ICalendarCacheRepository` + `CalendarCacheRepository` and a feature-disabled `CalendarCacheRepositoryMock` that explicitly no-ops `deleteManyByCredential`). Bypassing that repository creates a parallel, non-mockable path for cache deletion and risks behavior drift if the cache feature is disabled or the storage semantics change, even though the handler currently “works”.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] deleteCacheMutation's onSuccess shows a toast and calls onSuccess but never invalidates the connectedCalendars query, unlike disconnectMutation which invalidates in onSettled. After a user deletes cached data, the dropdown continues to display 'Last updated: <old timestamp>' from the stale tRPC cache until an unrelated refetch happens, making the delete appear to have done nothing to the very status indicator this feature adds.

adjudication.rationale: In `CredentialActionsDropdown.tsx`, `deleteCacheMutation` only shows a toast and calls `onSuccess?.()`; it does not invalidate/refetch any tRPC queries. By contrast, `disconnectMutation` explicitly invalidates `utils.viewer.calendars.connectedCalendars` (and integrations) in `onSettled`. Since `connectedCalendars.handler.ts` now enriches each calendar with `cacheUpdatedAt` from the DB, deleting cache via `deleteCache.handler.ts` would require a `connectedCalendars` refetch/invalidation to update the displayed `cacheUpdatedAt`; otherwise the dropdown can continue to show the old timestamp from the stale cached query result.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The migration backfills every legacy CalendarCache row with updatedAt = NOW() (the migration run time), which is a fabricated timestamp bearing no relation to when the cache entry was actually written. After deploy, every user with an existing cache sees 'Last updated: <deploy time>' — a misleading cache-status display that can hide genuinely stale caches, since nothing distinguishes a fresh entry from a legacy backfilled one.

adjudication.rationale: The diff introduces a new `CalendarCache.updatedAt` column and immediately exposes it in the UI as “Last updated” (`CredentialActionsDropdown.tsx` renders `cacheUpdatedAt`, which is populated from `CalendarCacheRepository.getCacheStatusByCredentialIds()` via `_max.updatedAt`). The migration adds the column as `NOT NULL DEFAULT NOW()` (`migration.sql`) and the Prisma model sets `@default(now()) @updatedAt`. For pre-existing `CalendarCache` rows, this will backfill `updatedAt` to the migration execution time (a fabricated value unrelated to when the cache entry was actually written), causing existing users to see “Last updated: <deploy time>” even for stale cache content. That matches the finding and is a correctness bug in the newly added cache-status display semantics.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] connectedCalendarsHandler always instantiates and calls CalendarCacheRepository.getCacheStatusByCredentialIds unconditionally, even in deployments where the calendar-cache feature is disabled (the repository mock exists solely for that case). Every connectedCalendars fetch on every settings/onboarding page load pays an extra groupBy query and enriches every calendar with a cacheUpdatedAt that the disabled feature never maintains, exposing a meaningless 'Last updated' timestamp to users of disabled-cache deployments.

adjudication.rationale: In `connectedCalendars.handler.ts`, the handler unconditionally `new CalendarCacheRepository()` and runs `getCacheStatusByCredentialIds` (a `prisma.calendarCache.groupBy` query) on every request, then enriches each calendar with `cacheUpdatedAt`. The diff shows a `CalendarCacheRepositoryMock` intended to “skip … due to calendar-cache being disabled”, but this handler does not select/use that mock or any feature flag, so deployments that conceptually have calendar-cache disabled would still pay the extra query (even if it returns `[]`). However, the finding’s claim that this necessarily “expos[es] a meaningless 'Last updated' timestamp” is not fully supported by the diff: the UI (`CredentialActionsDropdown`) only shows cache status when `cacheUpdatedAt` is truthy (`hasCache = isGoogleCalendar && cacheUpdatedAt`), so in many disabled-cache scenarios it would remain hidden.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] cacheUpdatedAt crosses the tRPC boundary where Dates are JSON-serialized to strings, but the prop is typed as Date | null and 'new Date(cacheUpdatedAt)' re-wraps it; the compile-time type asserts a type the wire format does not deliver. The prop's Date type is a lie on the client side; any future code treating it as a real Date (e.g. calling toISOString or date math on it without re-wrapping) breaks at runtime, and the re-wrapping in the render is load-bearing in a non-obvious way.

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds `cacheUpdatedAt` to the `connectedCalendars` tRPC response in `connectedCalendars.handler.ts` (derived from Prisma `updatedAt`, i.e. a `Date` on the server), and then consumes it in the client component `CredentialActionsDropdown` as `cacheUpdatedAt?: Date | null`, while rendering uses `new Date(cacheUpdatedAt)` before formatting. Across a tRPC JSON boundary, Dates are commonly serialized (often to strings) unless a Date-preserving transformer is configured (not shown in this diff), so the client-side `Date` type may be unsound and the current `new Date(...)` call becomes a non-obvious requirement. This is a concrete type-safety/maintainability issue, but not a clearly verifiable runtime bug from the diff alone.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] findMany drops the `satisfies Prisma.SelectedCalendarFindManyArgs` type check, silently weakening the compile-time contract on the args passed through to prisma. The next caller passing a malformed where/select now gets no type error at this boundary (previously caught by the satisfies clause), so a query-shape mistake surfaces only as a runtime Prisma error or as silently returning more columns than intended.

adjudication.rationale: In `SelectedCalendarRepository.findMany`, the diff changes from creating `args = { where, select, orderBy } satisfies Prisma.SelectedCalendarFindManyArgs` to passing the same object literal directly into `prisma.selectedCalendar.findMany({ where, select, orderBy })`. The Prisma client call still type-checks its argument against Prisma’s `findMany` args type at the callsite, so this change does not remove the compile-time contract at this boundary in a verifiable way based on the diff.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] deleteCacheHandler throws a plain Error('Credential not found or access denied') for a valid-but-unowned credentialId, which tRPC maps to a 500 INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR instead of a 4xx the client contract expects. A user probing another user's credentialId (or a stale UI after the credential was deleted) gets a generic 500 logged as a server error; the client's onError shows 'Error deleting cache' with no distinguishable cause, and error trackers fill with false-positive 500s from an expected authorization rejection.

adjudication.rationale: In `packages/trpc/server/routers/viewer/calendars/deleteCache.handler.ts`, the handler checks ownership via `prisma.credential.findFirst({ where: { id: credentialId, userId: user.id } })` and if missing throws a plain `new Error("Credential not found or access denied")`. In tRPC, an untyped thrown `Error` is typically mapped to a 500 `INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR` rather than an expected 4xx (e.g., `UNAUTHORIZED`/`FORBIDDEN`/`NOT_FOUND`). This means probing an unowned `credentialId` or a stale/deleted credential can produce a server-error 500 instead of a client-handled authorization/not-found response.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] deleteCacheMutation.onSuccess shows a toast and calls onSuccess but never invalidates utils.viewer.calendars.connectedCalendars, unlike the sibling disconnectMutation which invalidates it in onSettled. After deleting cache, the ConnectedCalendars query still holds the old cacheUpdatedAt, so the 'Last updated' row keeps displaying the pre-delete timestamp until some other action refetches — the success toast contradicts the visible state.

adjudication.rationale: In `CredentialActionsDropdown.tsx`, `deleteCacheMutation` only shows a toast and calls the optional `onSuccess?.()` callback; it does not invalidate/refetch `utils.viewer.calendars.connectedCalendars` (unlike `disconnectMutation`, which explicitly invalidates `connectedCalendars` in `onSettled`). Since `connectedCalendars.handler.ts` now derives `cacheUpdatedAt` from DB state, deleting rows via `deleteCache.handler.ts` would require a refetch to update the displayed `cache_last_updated`. The diff doesn’t show what the passed `onSuccess` does, so staleness is possible but not provable solely from this diff.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] connectedCalendarsHandler hard-instantiates `new CalendarCacheRepository()`, bypassing the repository-interface/mock abstraction the same PR extends (calendar-cache.repository.mock.ts returns [] precisely for the cache-disabled case). Every connectedCalendars fetch now runs an unconditional calendarCache.groupBy DB query even where the calendar-cache feature is disabled or mocked out; the DI seam the codebase maintains for this feature (interface + mock added in this diff) is silently skipped, so tests against the mock no longer reflect the real handler path and disabled-cache deployments pay a dead query on a hot settings-page path.

adjudication.rationale: In `packages/trpc/server/routers/viewer/calendars/connectedCalendars.handler.ts`, the handler directly imports and instantiates the concrete `CalendarCacheRepository` (`import { CalendarCacheRepository } ...` and `const cacheRepository = new CalendarCacheRepository();`), then unconditionally calls `getCacheStatusByCredentialIds(...)`, which in the implementation performs a Prisma `calendarCache.groupBy` query. This bypasses the `ICalendarCacheRepository` abstraction and the mock added/extended in this diff (`calendar-cache.repository.mock.ts`), so any intended DI seam for a cache-disabled/mock mode is not used by this handler. The claim about “feature disabled deployments” can’t be fully proven from the diff (no toggle shown), but the architectural/testability concern about skipping the interface/mock is directly supported by the change.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The new code updates SelectedCalendar.updatedAt for all calendars under the credential, but the cache-status UI introduced in this same PR reads CalendarCache.updatedAt (via getCacheStatusByCredentialIds), so the two halves of the feature target different tables. The updateManyByCredentialId write in fetchAvailabilityAndSetCache has no consumer in this diff's UI path — it mutates SelectedCalendar rows on every cron refresh, repurposing SelectedCalendar.updatedAt's meaning (selection-change timestamp) for cache bookkeeping nobody displays, while whoever later wires SelectedCalendar.updatedAt into the status card will double-count refreshes since CalendarCache.updatedAt is already maintained by @updatedAt on every setAvailabilityInCache upsert.

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows two separate cache-timestamp mechanisms: (1) UI cache status is sourced from CalendarCache.updatedAt via `CalendarCacheRepository.getCacheStatusByCredentialIds()` and `connectedCalendars.handler.ts` (adds `cacheUpdatedAt` from `calendarCache._max.updatedAt`), and (2) `GoogleCalendarService.fetchAvailabilityAndSetCache()` adds `SelectedCalendarRepository.updateManyByCredentialId(this.credential.id, {})` with a comment about updating `SelectedCalendar.updatedAt`. Nothing in this diff’s UI path reads `SelectedCalendar.updatedAt` for cache status, so that new updateMany call is currently unused from the introduced cache-status UI flow and creates a cross-table/semantics mismatch (even if future work might consume it). Parts of the finding about “repurposing meaning”/“double-count” are speculative beyond what the diff proves.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The timestamp is formatted with a hardcoded 'en-US' Intl.DateTimeFormat locale instead of the user's active locale from useLocale(). Non-English users see the only user-visible dynamic string in the dropdown rendered in US date/time format, contradicting the PR's own i18n setup (locale strings were added to common.json for every other label in this component).
matched_golden_ids: Date is formatted with hardcoded 'en-US' locale instead of using the user's locale from useLocale, which can lead to incorrect date representation for users in different locales.
adjudication_records.primary_judge_reasoning: The candidate issue flags the same problem: date/timestamp formatting uses a hardcoded 'en-US' locale instead of the user's locale from useLocale(), causing incorrect formatting for non-US users.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] cacheUpdatedAt is typed `Date | null` but arrives over the tRPC HTTP boundary as a serialized string, so `new Date(cacheUpdatedAt)` at line 106 relies on an untyped runtime value the declared type doesn't describe. Any consumer trusting the Date type (e.g. calling Date methods directly or passing the prop onward) hits runtime string behavior; the type lie propagates to every future caller of the component, and superjson-vs-JSON transport changes would silently alter what `new Date(cacheUpdatedAt)` receives.

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows `cacheUpdatedAt?: Date | null` passed from `connectedCalendars.handler.ts`, where it is sourced from Prisma (`_max.updatedAt`) and added to the returned tRPC payload. However, the finding’s core claim—that it “arrives over the tRPC HTTP boundary as a serialized string” (i.e., no superjson/Date transformer)—cannot be verified from this diff because no tRPC transformer/serialization configuration is shown. Also, within `CredentialActionsDropdown` the value is immediately wrapped in `new Date(cacheUpdatedAt)`, which works for both `Date` and ISO strings, so the diff does not demonstrate a concrete runtime breakage here.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The script uses `sed -i ''` (BSD/macOS-only syntax) and a CWD-relative ENV_FILE="../.env", so on Linux it rewrites the env file in-place incorrectly and from any directory other than scripts/ it edits the wrong .env. A developer running the script from the repo root on Linux gets a sed error or a corrupted .env line (sed treats '' as a filename), silently failing to point GOOGLE_WEBHOOK_URL at the tunnel and leaving gcal webhook testing broken with no visible error.

adjudication.rationale: In `scripts/test-gcal-webhooks.sh`, `ENV_FILE="../.env"` is relative to the current working directory, not the script location, so running it from repo root (or anywhere other than `scripts/`) will target the wrong `.env`. Also the script uses `sed -i '' -E ...`, which is BSD/macOS-style in-place editing; on GNU sed (Linux) the separate `''` is not valid as an optional `-i` argument and can be treated as a filename, causing an error (or preventing the replacement) rather than correctly editing the env file. Both issues are grounded in the added script and can break the intended behavior.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] deleteCacheHandler throws a plain Error('Credential not found or access denied') instead of a TRPCError, so an invalid credentialId surfaces as a generic 500 rather than a 4xx and the raw message can leak in the error response Any authenticated caller probing credentialIds gets a 500-with-message path indistinguishable from server failure; the error string is emitted to client-facing error payloads in the tRPC default error formatter, and operators get noise instead of a typed NOT_FOUND

adjudication.rationale: In `packages/trpc/server/routers/viewer/calendars/deleteCache.handler.ts`, when the credential is not found for the authed user, the handler does `throw new Error("Credential not found or access denied")`. In a tRPC mutation (`deleteCache` added in `_router.tsx`), throwing a plain `Error` will typically be treated as an untyped internal error (500) rather than a 4xx (e.g., NOT_FOUND/FORBIDDEN), and the message may be propagated through tRPC’s error payload/formatter. This is a real behavior issue introduced by the new endpoint.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The deleteCache mutation accepts any credentialId owned by the user but does not verify the credential is a Google Calendar credential, and the handler deletes only calendarCache rows without clearing the in-memory/availability cache path that CalendarService reads A user deleting cache for a non-calendar credential gets success:true with no effect, and for a Google credential the next availability fetch may still be served by layers outside calendarCache that the handler does not purge, so the 'delete cached data' UI action is not a complete invalidation

adjudication.rationale: In `packages/trpc/server/routers/viewer/calendars/deleteCache.handler.ts`, the mutation only verifies the credential exists and is owned by the user (`prisma.credential.findFirst({ where: { id: credentialId, userId: user.id } })`) and then deletes `calendarCache` rows via `prisma.calendarCache.deleteMany({ where: { credentialId } })`. There is no check that the credential is actually a Google Calendar credential/integration type, so calling the mutation with a non-calendar credentialId would still return `{ success: true }` (likely deleting 0 rows). The claim about other in-memory/availability cache layers not being purged is not directly verifiable from this diff (only DB cache deletion is shown), but the missing type validation and “success with no effect” scenario are diff-grounded completeness concerns.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The DEFAULT NOW() backfill stamps every legacy CalendarCache row with the migration-execution time, so pre-existing caches instantly appear 'fresh' as of deploy time. Users with stale cache entries see 'Last updated: <migration timestamp>' in the new cache-status UI and believe their availability data was just refreshed, defeating the purpose of the feature for all pre-existing rows; correct behavior would require seeding updatedAt from the cache creation signal (e.g. expiresAt minus TTL) rather than NOW(). No data is lost and the migration itself is reversible (DROP COLUMN), so this is not blocking.

adjudication.rationale: The migration adds `CalendarCache.updatedAt` as `NOT NULL DEFAULT NOW()` (migration.sql) and the Prisma model sets `updatedAt @default(now()) @updatedAt`. The new UI/endpoint uses the cache row’s `updatedAt` as “Last updated” via `CalendarCacheRepository.getCacheStatusByCredentialIds()` (groupBy `_max.updatedAt`) and `connectedCalendars.handler.ts` maps that into `cacheUpdatedAt`, which `CredentialActionsDropdown` formats and displays. For pre-existing `CalendarCache` rows, the ALTER TABLE default will stamp them with the migration execution time, making old caches appear freshly updated in the UI, which is a correctness issue for the “cache status” feature.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] updateManyByCredentialId is called with an empty data object ({}), relying entirely on Prisma's implicit @updatedAt behavior on SelectedCalendar to bump the timestamp — if SelectedCalendar.updatedAt lacks @updatedAt in the schema, the call is a silent no-op write. The CalendarService refresh hook (CalendarService.ts line ~1022) intends to mark all SelectedCalendars under the credential as refreshed; if the model's updatedAt is a plain DateTime without @updatedAt, Prisma rejects or ignores empty update data and SelectedCalendar.updatedAt never advances, so any future consumer reading SelectedCalendar.updatedAt (it is now surfaced in getConnectedDestinationCalendars and UserRepository select) sees stale timestamps. Verify @updatedAt is present on SelectedCalendar.updatedAt.

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows `CalendarService.updateAvailabilityInCache()` now calls `SelectedCalendarRepository.updateManyByCredentialId(this.credential.id, {})`, i.e., an `updateMany` with an empty `data` object, apparently to bump `SelectedCalendar.updatedAt` for all calendars under the credential. However, the diff does not show the `SelectedCalendar` model in `schema.prisma`, so it’s not verifiable here whether `SelectedCalendar.updatedAt` has `@updatedAt` (or whether Prisma allows/meaningfully executes an empty update). This is a concrete, diff-grounded concern about relying on implicit ORM behavior that may be a no-op or error if the schema/Prisma semantics don’t support it, but it can’t be confirmed as a definite defect from the provided diff alone.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] deleteCacheHandler throws a plain Error('Credential not found or access denied') when the credential lookup misses, which tRPC surfaces as a 500 INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR instead of the 404/403 the situation calls for. A user (or a stale client holding a deleted credentialId) triggering 'Delete cached data' gets a generic server-error toast and a 5xx logged server-side for what is an expected not-found/forbidden case; error monitoring is polluted with non-exception failures.

adjudication.rationale: In `packages/trpc/server/routers/viewer/calendars/deleteCache.handler.ts`, when the credential is not found/owned (`findFirst` returns null), the handler does `throw new Error("Credential not found or access denied")`. In a tRPC `mutation` (wired in `_router.tsx` via `authedProcedure`), throwing a plain `Error` is surfaced as an `INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR` (5xx) rather than an appropriate `NOT_FOUND`/`FORBIDDEN`/`UNAUTHORIZED` typed error. This turns an expected user-facing case (stale/deleted `credentialId` or forbidden access) into a server error and matches the finding.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] deleteCacheMutation has no onSettled invalidation of viewer.calendars.connectedCalendars, so the displayed 'Last updated' timestamp stays stale unless the parent happens to pass an onSuccess prop that refetches. Any consumer of CredentialActionsDropdown that omits onSuccess (the prop is optional) shows the old cache timestamp after a successful delete until an unrelated refetch occurs, making the user believe the delete did nothing.

adjudication.rationale: In `CredentialActionsDropdown.tsx`, `deleteCacheMutation` only shows a toast and calls optional `onSuccess?.()`; it does not invalidate/refetch `viewer.calendars.connectedCalendars` (unlike `disconnectMutation`, which invalidates onSettled). Since the displayed `cacheUpdatedAt` comes from the `cacheUpdatedAt` prop (fed by `connectedCalendars.handler.ts` enrichment), any consumer that omits `onSuccess` will keep rendering the old `Last updated` timestamp after a successful delete until some unrelated refetch occurs, making the UI stale/misleading.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] connectedCalendarsHandler directly instantiates CalendarCacheRepository instead of going through the calendar-cache feature factory, bypassing the CalendarCacheRepositoryMock used when the feature is disabled. When calendar-cache is disabled the handler still issues a groupBy query against calendarCache on every connectedCalendars fetch, and the disabled-mode contract ('skip and log') documented in calendar-cache.repository.mock.ts is silently not honored; deployments with the feature off pay a DB round-trip per settings/onboarding page load for data that is always empty.

adjudication.rationale: In `packages/trpc/server/routers/viewer/calendars/connectedCalendars.handler.ts`, the handler imports and directly instantiates `new CalendarCacheRepository()` and calls `getCacheStatusByCredentialIds`, which in `calendar-cache.repository.ts` always executes a Prisma `groupBy` on `calendarCache`. The diff also adds `CalendarCacheRepositoryMock.getCacheStatusByCredentialIds()` that explicitly logs and returns `[]` when “calendar-cache [is] disabled”, implying there is an intended disabled-mode pathway. This handler does not appear to use any abstraction/factory that could swap in the mock, so if the feature is disabled via such a mechanism elsewhere, this change would bypass it and still hit the DB per request.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] Every getAvailability path now performs an unconditional updateMany write across all SelectedCalendar rows for the credential, even when availability was served from a still-valid cache and nothing was refreshed. Read-path availability checks turn into N-row writes on each call, adding DB write load and constantly churning SelectedCalendar.updatedAt for every calendar under the credential, degrading any other consumer that relies on updatedAt as a change signal.

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds an unconditional `SelectedCalendarRepository.updateManyByCredentialId(this.credential.id, {})` at the end of the Google Calendar availability/caching flow (`CalendarService.ts` right after the cache-hit/refresh conditional). `updateManyByCredentialId` is implemented as `prisma.selectedCalendar.updateMany({ where: { credentialId }, data })`, so this introduces a write query on every call through this path, including when cached availability was used. The comment explicitly indicates the intent is to bump `SelectedCalendar.updatedAt` for all calendars under the credential, which would indeed churn `updatedAt` and add DB write load on what is otherwise a read/cache-hit path.
